analysis.one_liner: Sets FDA limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in baby food.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on July 23, 2024, and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA to set legal limits on four toxic heavy metals — lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury — in food made for babies and toddlers, and in fruit and vegetable purees and juices. Companies making those foods would have to test their finished products at least every three months, keep records of the results, and run sanitation monitoring programs for pathogens in their plants. Foods exceeding the limits would count as adulterated under federal law, and the FDA would gain authority to order recalls and to obtain company records without an on-site inspection.
analysis.who_benefits: Infants and toddlers, whose developing bodies are most vulnerable to heavy metals like lead and arsenic, and their parents, who would get enforceable contaminant limits and regular testing instead of relying on company goodwill. Because the FDA's limits would also apply to imported foods and importers would have to verify testing records, families would also get more assurance about foreign-made baby food.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and infants eating store-bought baby food

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to set binding limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food and in fruit and vegetable purees and juices, with proposed orders due between December 2025 and April 2028 and final orders 18 months after each proposal.

Requires manufacturers to test finished baby food products for those metals at least quarterly under a written sampling plan, using accredited laboratories, and to keep the results available to the FDA for at least two years.

Makes any baby food exceeding the limits legally adulterated, creates a prohibited act for failing to comply with the testing and record rules, and extends the FDA's existing mandatory recall authority to foods that are adulterated.

Requires FDA to finalize an implementation plan for its food traceability rule, study how many inspections of imported food are needed to hold imports to domestic standards, and report annually on inspection findings and importer compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Baby food manufacturers and fruit and vegetable puree and juice producers would bear the cost of quarterly accredited laboratory testing, written sampling plans, recordkeeping, environmental monitoring programs, and reformulating or sourcing cleaner ingredients where the limits require it. Those costs could be passed on to consumers in higher prices. The FDA would also need funding and staff to write the orders and verify compliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Baby food and puree manufacturers, and ultimately shoppers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for quarterly accredited testing, recordkeeping, and environmental monitoring would fall on manufacturers and could raise baby food prices for the families the bill is meant to help.

The bill itself directs the FDA to account for heavy metals that cannot be avoided in production when setting limits, acknowledging that some contaminants come from soil and water and that zero contamination is not achievable, so the limits would not eliminate exposure.

The timeline is slow: proposed mercury limits were not required until April 2028 and final orders could come 18 months after each proposal, and testing requirements would not begin until two years after enactment, so protection would be years away even if it had passed.

The bill adds significant new mandates to the FDA without providing additional funding, raising the question of whether the agency could write the orders and run the independent verification program on its existing budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — enforceable limits on lead and other neurotoxic metals in food for children under two — is significant, because there is no known safe level of lead exposure for young children. The main costs are compliance expenses that could nudge prices up and an implementation timeline that stretches years into the future. On balance the protections outweigh the costs, though the bill's slow phase-in and unfunded mandates are real weaknesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2024 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never held a markup or hearing, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 in the House on July 23, 2024, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Tony Cardenas.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no companion Senate action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Baby food manufacturers and puree and juice producers are better off, because they avoided mandatory contaminant limits, quarterly product testing, and environmental monitoring requirements. Families with young children got no new protection against heavy metals in baby food.

for.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

for.name: Tony Cardenas
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: House committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, no roll-call votes were ever taken, and no Republican opposition was formally recorded — the bill simply was never considered by the Republican-led committee.

industries.note: The bill would require binding limits on four heavy metals in their products, quarterly accredited testing of finished food, two years of recordkeeping, and plant sanitation monitoring, with adulterated products subject to mandatory recall. Their interest in avoiding these mandates runs against parents' interest in limiting infants' exposure to lead and arsenic.

industries.industry: Fruit and vegetable puree and juice producers
industries.note: The same contaminant limits, testing, and record rules would apply to foods mostly made of fruit or vegetable purees and juices, adding compliance costs. Their interest in avoiding the mandates runs against the public's interest in lower heavy metal exposure.

The bill would require all sampling and testing to be performed by accredited labs meeting international standards, creating steady new demand for testing services. This interest runs alongside the public's interest in reliable contamination data.

Importers would have to monitor and verify the accuracy of testing records for covered foods, and the bill pushes FDA to study how many inspections are needed to hold imports to domestic standards. Added verification costs, but the public gains confidence that imported baby food meets the same limits.
